quick fun little game for time-killing purposes. definitely feels like it's a bit lacking in features i won't lie, but as an easy to pick up/come back to time-killing game for word nerds specifically? it's nice enough and has a solid variety of things to do with the concept.

it could be better, and if you're looking for a particularly in-depth mix of RPG elements and typing/boggle-esque gameplay, this probably won't do it for you (the buffs from the Blacksmith and, to *some* extent, the effects of the character's attacks are rarely all that consequential, though you'd probably want a healing ability and an enemy freezing ability of some sort). hell, the game's "runs" don't even end; they just go on and on until you wipe, which can sometimes take ages. but you can always pause and come back to the run in a later session; so, honestly, i almost think it's good that it doesn't end if, again, you play this as a time-killing game.

as far as things to work toward across runs: the character unlocking/levelling, bestiary, and unique words counter all offer things to work toward, either finite or... i guess as big as whatever dictionary this game pulls from (which, i will also note, sometimes pulls from some rather obscure/esoteric words, or, conversely, is a bit behind on modern lingo).

so, regardless of its lack of depth, i find myself coming back to this game pretty often in those "idk what to do and don't have the mental capacity to do much of anything productive" moments, and i have more than gotten my money's worth in that department. the presentation is also pretty nice in my opinion, with nice pixel art and framing, and the game window being small (and not needing to be larger*) helps keep it unobtrusive when doing other things alongside it.

[i]*NOTE: i believe, from what i've seen from some other reviews, that this can be a problem for larger monitors, ie 4K resolution monitors, due to the window size being uncustomizable (at least through normal means). keep that in mind[/i]

also the game is a bit funny in certain understated ways. Santa Claus being a character was funny enough, but one of his attacks essentially being a coin flip to judge your opponent either naughty or nice (with "naughty" dealing damage to them, and "nice" healing them) is something i get a kick out of every time i come across him

if what i've described here sounds good to you, give it a shot (maybe wait for a sale if you're skeptical). you'll know soon enough whether you'll like having a game like this sitting in your steam library *far* before reaching 2 hours of playtime, anyway, so there's not much risk

In WORDS OF EVIL, the aim is to lead a party of up to 3 adventurers through various lands while defeating deadly creatures, finding treasure, and avoiding traps.  Unlike most standard RPG games, however, here the arena is not a sprawling dungeon but a grid of 35 squares each representing a random letter of the alphabet!

After selecting an initial party, the characters go on a "run" across the landscape where random encounters could lead to shrines for statistic improvement, treasure chests, vicious traps, equipment shops to buy new items, or monsters.  These events are randomised so no two journeys will ever be the same!

Meeting a monster invokes a battle to the death.  Here the letter grid will appear.  Enemies are "hit" by creating words from selected letter tiles with those adjacent to it - including diagonally - and the longer the word then the more damage that will be inflicted to the enemy health bar.  Monsters hit back at certain periods, gradually reducing health from our characters, with stronger foes attacking much more frequently.  Once words are created the tiles disappear and new ones take their place, ensuring there are always 35 letters in play.

When an enemy is killed we receive gold and experience, then immediately travel onwards to the next encounter.  Gold may be spent at any of the shops we find along the way while experience allows us to level up our characters once enough is gained.

Sometimes we encounter traps and here we are presented with an anagram of several letter tiles in which to create a single word.  Successfully using every letter shall disarm the trap but smaller words will result in health damage to our characters.  Likewise, chests have a couple of tile rows and by combining the letters in sequence to spell a word will open it and distribute a reward.  Both the trap and chest challenges are timed.

Each character has 3 battle abilities which are unlocked by questing.  These are Basic, Strong and Ultra, and come into play depending on how many tiles are used to form words.  Ultra attacks obviously do massive amounts of damage to a monster while the others do considerably less.  Various tiles are colour coded for additional bonuses, too.

If a character is defeated in battle they are given a "last chance" of survival with a challenge by solving a 7 letter anagram.  Doing so returns them to the fight with full health.  Completing smaller words may increase half their health, but tiny words usually result in the character being killed, although the enemy will suffer a little damage as well.  Fortunately fallen heroes are available for the next "run" with all their skills and experience level still intact.  Therefore some grind is inevitable to produce veteran adventurers who will be able to take on the strongest creatures in the game.

We are able to unlock 19 heroes, from sword masters and archers to the likes of snowmen and even Santa Claus!  There are 84 different monsters to face throughout 7 lands of increasing difficulty.  No matter which land we choose or monster we fight, though, each "run" follows the same basic formula.

I quite enjoy WORDS OF EVIL as it offers a new approach to the standard RPG genre.  It obviously helps if we like word games, too!  There are sadly no Achievements but a total of 6 Trading Cards to collect.

A slight downside is that there is no full screen mode available and thus the game is played within a window, ensuring the graphics are quite small (but still functionable) and this does not distract too much from the overall game.  Indeed, it can be both fast and exciting within its own limited framework structure.

Anybody wanting something a little different should certainly give it a try!

Words for Evil is like if Scrabble and a fantasy RPG had a baby, and that baby drank way too much coffee. It mostly does what it promises, and the graphics are nice enough to make you think you’re playing a retro classic… until you remember you're just trying to spell “cat” under pressure.

The RPG elements? Well, let’s just say they’re as minimal as my gym attendance. You’ll find yourself battling enemies and leveling up, but don’t expect an epic quest or a deep narrative—it's more like a wordy scavenger hunt gone rogue.

The gameplay is very repetitive, but if you fall into the game loop, be prepared to lose hours of your life that no one is giving you back. 

 At some point, I just decided to throw in the towel and return to games with actual stories—like, you know, anything with a plot.

In the end, the pixel art is delightful, but it’s not enough to save the day. So if you’re ready for a wordy adventure that might just turn your brain into scrambled eggs, dive in. Just don’t say I didn’t warn you!

If you want to play a fun rpg game, this is not it. This is a masochistic crossword puzzle. Whenever people say there is no word for the day after tomorrow, and make fun of defenestration for being present in the language, I am quick to make them regret their poor existence by explaining a. overmorrow exists, and so does ereyesterday, the day before yesterday; and b. defenestration describes historically significant events occurring 199 years apart in the Prague castle. Defenestration isn't even exclusive to the english language at all. Three plurals of octopus exist, the latinized octopi, most commonly taught, the obscure but appropriately greek octopodes, but despite these, the most commonly used word is octopuses. Isn't that neat? Why are you still reading this?

Words for Evil - rogue-like word game. With some basic 'RPG' (in terms of Rogue-like) elements and the word-connecting basic gameplay mechanic. The thing I really liked is that the game actually aims to develop your vocabulary, explains things, and instigate, relish the player to continue the journey, open some new characters, new lands, new types of monsters... And new words, of course!

However, there are some itches that stop me from declaring my love for this game worldwide. 

First of all, while a rogue-like basis is really suitable for this game, I am well aware that not all players around like such games. I am not too fond of rogue-likes myself, actually. And there we have a combo of two not-so-popular-and-kinda-boring-for-many-people genres, which makes the audience interest even rarer, in big numbers. Negative multiplication, ever heard of such a concept in your lessons of Economics?

Also, the visuals are bad. I mean, it's not completely bad, maybe even quite typical, for a rogue-like... But considering the fact that it is a words game, where you need to look for possible letter connotations all the way... Well, yeah, it's bad.

Finally, the timed game basis actually pushes you to look for the shortest 3-4-letters words, with only the rare occasions to make longer combinations. Plus, again, the size of the whole game screen and the tablet with the letters, ain't really helping for quick long words searches. So, after a short while, even the native English speakers will usually use 3-letter-words. The same but worse goes for those like me, who wasn't hearing English words from an early age and therefore have a shorter passive/active vocabulary.

So, while I'm still quite positive about this game in general, I can't really recommend it to my kids, and I'll not be playing it much myself. It's a good words game, but not the best one, even considering the fact there are only a few of them on the market. Speaking of the overall mark, let's say 6.5/10. Definitely not bad, but leaves quite a room to dream of better execution.

Зато можно собирать не только по горизонтали/вертикали, но и по диагонали, причем, комбинируя все эти способы в пределах одного слова. Ну и помимо основных словесных боев есть еще две мини-игры с поиском слов, правда тоже на время.
И все-таки хотелось бы что-то подобное на русском языке.

As someone whose primary language isn't English, I bought this game to improve my vocabulary.
I thought playing an RPG +Word Puzzle would provide a fun way to improve my English. Much like The Typing of The Dead helped me type without looking at the keyboard.

But this game didn't help. Not only did it not help, I didn't find the game to be much fun.

Your character is on a trail. You keep moving forward, endlessly and aimlessly, encountering enemies, traps, shops and healers.

Enemies attack you every few seconds with an annoying Thud sound.
Traps can take half of your HP if you don't diffuse them.
Shops and Healers are found so far between and you usually find yourself low on coin for even a Heal!

None of them are much fun, but the worst part of the game is the words used in the puzzle.
The number of letters and the templates given cause you to have to make small words. How small? 3 letter words.
And you haven't heard half the words that this game accepts in your entire life! Even as an USA/UK grown person.

Here are some of the words I found that could give an image as to what I mean:
Pax, ped, nat, soe, ree, fid, hae, bap, rud, tay, sous, apert, rore, mog, res, tui, spar, rom, tel, tole, lat, fop, sol, reak, tew, fab, rue, sos, kep, wee, tot, tam, rye

What the hell do any of them mean I have no idea.
All these stupid, never heard before words...but "crap" is not accepted.

And as I said, with the templates and number of letters given, you will mostly be writing 3 letter words from above.

words of evil, is in some ways, akin to letter quest. a word game in essence, coupled with tinges of an rpg. unlike letter quest, this game is made of pixel art (fairly well done if i may say so), with a simple, but nice enough to be effective soundtrack.

you start off with a small selection of characters (which will grow as you find them through the game, and unlock them), with their own unique abilities. you battle through the world, leveling your characters, and collecting equipment which will in turn, boost their stats.

as you play on, you will unlock a huge selection of characters, with their own unique abilities. you trigger these abilities, by forming words using colored blocks that correspond to the character's color.

while the game has that interesting rpg mechanic tied to it, the real problem lies with the combat. it's fairly difficult to keep track of damage dealt, and damage received, as more than half the time, you're actually trying to look at the board and figure out what words you can piece together. unlike letter quest where you and the enemy take turns to move, the real-time battle mechanics here makes everything a bit messy.

to be fair though, while damage does kill your characters, and thus making it seem pretty bad that damage tracking is so messy, you are given a chance to keep your character alive every time they take critical damage (damage that kills them). i must admit it makes it fairly easy to 'cheat' if one is so inclined.

all in all, words of evil is a pretty good game. it does have it's quirks for better or for worse, but in general, its a pretty solid time killer. it just feels like they could have done a bit more, but as it is, and for the price, it's a pretty good value buy.
